FreshLLMs: Refreshing Large Language Models with Search Engine Augmentation [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
Tu Vu, Mohit Iyyer, Xuezhi Wang, Noah Constant, Jerry Wei, Jason Wei, Chris Tar, Yun-Hsuan Sung, Denny Zhou, Quoc Le, Thang Luong [S2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03214)
arXiv:2310.03214v2
Abstract: Most large language models (LLMs) are trained once and never updated; thus, they lack the ability to dynamically adapt to our ever-changing world. In this work, we perform a detailed study of the factuality of LLM-generated text in the context of answering questions that test current world knowledge. Specifically, we introduce FreshQA, a novel dynamic QA benchmark encompassing a diverse range of question and answer types, including questions that involve fast-changing world knowledge as well as questions with false premises that need to be debunked. We benchmark a wide range of both closed and open-source LLMs under a two-mode evaluation procedure that allows us to measure both correctness and hallucination. Through human evaluations involving more than 50K judgments, we shed light on limitations of these models and demonstrate significant room for improvement: for instance, all models (regardless of model size) struggle on questions that involve fast-changing knowledge and false premises. Motivated by these findings, we present FreshPrompt, a simple few-shot prompting method that substantially boosts the performance of an LLM on FreshQA by incorporating relevant and up-to-date information retrieved from a search engine into the prompt. Our experiments show that FreshPrompt outperforms competing search engine-augmented prompting methods such as Self-ask(Press et al., [2022](#bib.bib27)) as well as commercial systems such as [this http URL]( (e.g., Perplexity.AI). Further analysis of FreshPrompt reveals that both the number of retrieved evidences and their order play a key role in influencing the correctness of LLM-generated answers. Additionally, instructing the LLM to generate concise and direct answers helps reduce hallucination compared to encouraging more verbose answers. To facilitate future work, we release FreshQA at [github.com/freshllms/freshqa]( and commit to updating it at regular intervals. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
## 1 Introduction
In this section, we describe the motivation, background, and contributions of our work. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
### 1.1 Motivation
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a wide range of tasks, from natural language understanding to code generation. However, their performance is often limited by the static nature of their training data, which may not reflect the rapidly changing world. This limitation is particularly evident in tasks that require up-to-date knowledge, such as answering questions about current events or recent developments. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
### 1.2 Background
Previous work has explored various approaches to address the static nature of LLMs, including fine-tuning on new data, using retrieval-augmented generation, and incorporating external knowledge sources. However, these methods often require significant computational resources and may not be easily adaptable to new domains or tasks. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
### 1.3 Contributions
In this paper, we introduce FreshQA, a novel dynamic QA benchmark that challenges LLMs to answer questions that require up-to-date knowledge. We also present FreshPrompt, a simple few-shot prompting method that leverages search engine results to improve the factuality of LLM-generated answers. Our experiments demonstrate that FreshPrompt significantly outperforms competing methods and provides a promising direction for future research in this area. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
## 2 Related Work
We review related work on dynamic QA benchmarks, retrieval-augmented generation, and few-shot prompting. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
## 3 FreshQA: A Dynamic QA Benchmark
We describe the construction of FreshQA, including the collection of questions, the annotation process, and the evaluation protocol. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
## 4 FreshPrompt: A Simple Few-Shot Prompting Method
We present FreshPrompt, a method that incorporates search engine results into the prompt to improve the factuality of LLM-generated answers. We discuss the design of FreshPrompt, its implementation, and its advantages over competing methods. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
## 5 Experiments
We evaluate FreshPrompt on FreshQA and compare it to competing methods. We also analyze the impact of different factors, such as the number of retrieved evidences and the order of the evidences, on the performance of FreshPrompt. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)
## 6 Conclusion
We conclude by summarizing our findings and discussing future directions for research in this area. [S1](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03214v1)

details.question: PostgreSQL 官方文档中，`synchronous_commit=remote_apply` 会让 COMMIT 等待到什么状态？这对只读查询的可见性意味着什么？
details.reference_answer: `remote_apply` 会让每次提交等待当前同步备库确认已经重放该事务；因此事务随后对备库上的用户查询可见。
details.model_answer:
When `synchronous_commit=remote_apply` is set, a `COMMIT` will wait for the synchronous standby to acknowledge that the transaction has been applied (i.e., the data is visible on the standby). If the primary receives a cancellation signal (e.g., `CTRL+C` or a client abort), PostgreSQL will still report success locally but will issue a warning: [S2](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/cac4b9df-92c6-77aa-687b-18b86cb13728@stratox.cz)
> "WARNING: canceling wait for synchronous replication due to user request [S2](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/cac4b9df-92c6-77aa-687b-18b86cb13728@stratox.cz)
> DETAIL: The transaction has already committed locally, but might not have been replicated to the standby." [S2](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/cac4b9df-92c6-77aa-687b-18b86cb13728@stratox.cz)
This means the transaction is committed on the primary, but the standby may not yet have received or applied it. [S1](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/84cc0332fadf4f4bb1fff7a169db8ecd58f7911c.camel%40cybertec.at)
**Implications for read-only queries:** [S1](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/84cc0332fadf4f4bb1fff7a169db8ecd58f7911c.camel%40cybertec.at)
Because the transaction is considered committed on the primary, read-only queries on the primary will see the new data. However, if the primary fails and a standby is promoted, the standby may not have received the transaction (if the cancellation occurred before the standby acknowledged it). In that case, the promoted standby will not contain the transaction, and read-only queries on the new primary will not see the data. Thus, the transaction is not guaranteed to be visible to all readers in a failover scenario. [S1](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/84cc0332fadf4f4bb1fff7a169db8ecd58f7911c.camel%40cybertec.at)

details.model_answer: SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of the original SWE-bench dataset, consisting of 500 samples that evaluate AI models’ ability to solve real-world software issues. The dataset was curated through a rigorous human annotation process involving 93 software developers. Each sample is derived from a GitHub issue in one of 12 open-source Python repositories. Each sample has an associated pull request (PR), which includes both the solution code and unit tests that validate the solution. These unit tests are known as `FAIL_TO_PASS` tests. The dataset was created to address issues with the original SWE-bench, such as underspecified problem statements and unit tests that may unfairly mark valid solutions as incorrect. The annotation process involved three separate annotators to ensure the issue description is well-specified, the unit tests are appropriate, and the sample is free of other major issues. The dataset is available for download. [S2](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified)
